Front: Why restart and run all cells before sharing?
Back: To detect hidden execution-order dependencies and missing setup.

Front: Python environments and notebooks: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Installing into the wrong interpreter or relying on stale notebook variables.

Front: Does a Python type hint validate runtime values?
Back: No; explicit validation or a library is needed.

Front: Python data types, control flow and functions: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Mutable default arguments can retain state across calls.

Front: What dimensions can broadcast?
Back: Equal dimensions or a dimension of size one, aligned from the right.

Front: NumPy arrays, broadcasting and vectorization: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Dividing by zero or silently broadcasting along the wrong axis.

Front: Why inspect join cardinality?
Back: To prevent accidental row multiplication or lost records.

Front: Pandas, data cleaning and EDA: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Many-to-many joins can unexpectedly multiply rows; test-set exploration can bias model selection.

Front: What should an experiment record besides the seed?
Back: Code version, data version, dependency versions, parameters and metrics.

Front: Git, testing and reproducible experiments: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Committing credentials or assuming seeds alone guarantee reproducibility.

Front: When is cosine similarity undefined?
Back: When either vector has zero norm.

Front: Linear algebra: vectors, matrices and dot products: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Confusing elementwise multiplication with matrix multiplication or ignoring zero norms.

Front: What does PCA maximize?
Back: Variance captured by orthogonal components of centered data.

Front: Eigenvalues, SVD and projections: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: PCA components depend on scaling and do not necessarily preserve predictive information.

Front: Why does prevalence matter?
Back: The posterior combines the likelihood with the prior probability.

Front: Probability, distributions and Bayes rule: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Confusing P(test positive given condition) with P(condition given test positive).

Front: What does 95% confidence mean?
Back: Under repeated valid sampling, the interval procedure covers the parameter about 95% of the time.

Front: Statistics, sampling and confidence intervals: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Ignoring dependence, selection bias or nonrepresentative samples.

Front: Why is the chain rule essential to neural networks?
Back: It propagates gradients through composed layers.

Front: Calculus, gradients and optimization: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: A learning rate that is too large can overshoot or diverge.

Front: Is KL divergence symmetric?
Back: No, swapping the distributions generally changes the result.

Front: Information theory and numerical stability: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Taking log(0) or applying softmax twice before a logits-based loss.

Front: Why use a baseline?
Back: To quantify whether additional modeling complexity improves outcomes.

Front: ML problem framing and baselines: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Choosing an algorithm before defining the target or using information unavailable at prediction time.

Front: Should scalers be fit before the split?
Back: No, fit them on training data only.

Front: Train, validation, test and leakage: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Feature leakage from future data, repeated entities or target-derived columns.

Front: Why put preprocessing inside cross-validation?
Back: Each fold must learn preprocessing only from its training partition.

Front: Preprocessing and feature pipelines: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Unknown categories at inference or fitting preprocessing using the whole dataset.

Front: What does a residual represent?
Back: Observed target minus predicted target.

Front: Linear and polynomial regression: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: High-degree polynomials can overfit; correlation is not causal effect.

Front: What changes when the threshold changes?
Back: Class decisions and confusion-matrix metrics, not the fitted probability model.

Front: Logistic regression and classification thresholds: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Treating probabilities as calibrated without checking or optimizing accuracy for rare positives.

Front: Which models are sensitive to feature scale?
Back: Distance-based kNN and many SVM configurations.

Front: k-nearest neighbors, naive Bayes and SVM: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Unscaled features dominate distances; kernel SVM can be expensive on large data.

Front: How does bagging reduce variance?
Back: It averages diverse estimators whose errors are not perfectly correlated.

Front: Decision trees and random forests: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Unconstrained trees memorize training data; impurity importance can favor high-cardinality features.

Front: What is the key difference between bagging and boosting?
Back: Bagging aggregates independently trained models; boosting fits learners sequentially to improve the current ensemble.

Front: Gradient boosting: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Using early stopping on test data or encoding categories inconsistently.

Front: Does regularization always improve performance?
Back: No; excessive regularization can cause underfitting.

Front: Regularization, feature selection and bias-variance: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Selecting features using all targets before cross-validation leaks information.

Front: Why can accuracy be misleading under imbalance?
Back: A majority-class predictor can score highly while missing nearly all positives.

Front: Classification, regression and ranking metrics: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: AUC does not identify an operating threshold and accuracy can hide minority failures.

Front: What is nested CV for?
Back: Estimating generalization of a model-selection procedure without using outer folds for tuning.

Front: Cross-validation and hyperparameter search: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Repeatedly tuning against the final test set invalidates it.

Front: What does a calibrated 0.8 probability mean?
Back: Among comparable predictions near 0.8, roughly 80% should be positive.

Front: Imbalanced learning, calibration and uncertainty: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Oversampling before splitting leaks duplicate or related rows; calibration requires separate data or folds.

Front: Can SHAP prove a feature causes an outcome?
Back: No, model attribution is not causal identification.

Front: Interpretability, fairness and error analysis: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Treating feature attribution as causality or reporting only aggregate accuracy.

Front: Why might DBSCAN label points as noise?
Back: They are not density-reachable under the selected parameters.

Front: Clustering: k-means, hierarchical and DBSCAN: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Treating clusters as true labels or relying on a single internal score.

Front: Should t-SNE cluster distances be treated as exact original distances?
Back: No; global geometry can be distorted.

Front: Dimensionality reduction: PCA, t-SNE and UMAP: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Interpreting all distances and cluster sizes in t-SNE as meaningful.

Front: What is novelty detection?
Back: Scoring new observations against a model of normal training data.

Front: Anomaly detection and novelty detection: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Training on future incidents or assuming every anomaly is malicious.

Front: Why use rolling-origin evaluation?
Back: It simulates repeated forecasts using only historical information.

Front: Time series, forecasting and backtesting: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Random splitting or calculating rolling features that include future observations.

Front: Why use candidate retrieval before ranking?
Back: It reduces the number of items requiring expensive ranking.

Front: Recommendation and learning to rank: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Random negative sampling can misrepresent unseen relevance and cold-start performance.

Front: Can accurate prediction establish causality?
Back: No; causal claims need a valid identification strategy.

Front: Causal inference and experimentation: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Conditioning on post-treatment variables or repeatedly peeking at p-values without adjustment.

Front: Why zero gradients before a training step?
Back: PyTorch accumulates gradients rather than replacing them automatically.

Front: Tensors, autograd and PyTorch fundamentals: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: In-place mutation of tracked tensors or mixing CPU and GPU tensors.

Front: Why are nonlinear activations needed?
Back: Without them, stacked linear layers cannot represent nonlinear decision boundaries.

Front: Perceptrons, MLPs and activation functions: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Applying sigmoid to logits before BCEWithLogitsLoss or using incompatible target shape.

Front: Does backpropagation update weights itself?
Back: No; it computes gradients that an optimizer uses to update weights.

Front: Forward pass, backpropagation and loss functions: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Detaching a tensor breaks its gradient path; incorrect logits/target shapes can silently mislead.

Front: What does AdamW decouple?
Back: Weight decay from the adaptive gradient update.

Front: Optimizers, initialization and learning-rate schedules: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Confusing L2 regularization with decoupled weight decay for adaptive optimizers.

Front: Why use model.eval() plus no_grad or inference_mode?
Back: They control module behavior and gradient recording separately.

Front: Datasets, DataLoaders and training loops: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Forgetting eval mode changes dropout and batch normalization behavior.

Front: Why can dropout predictions differ in training mode?
Back: Random activation masks are sampled during training.

Front: Normalization, dropout and early stopping: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Evaluating with dropout active or selecting checkpoints using test loss.

Front: What is data-parallel training?
Back: Replicas process different data batches and synchronize gradients.

Front: Mixed precision, GPUs and distributed training: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Assuming lower precision is always faster or forgetting effective batch size changes.

Front: Why use weight sharing in CNNs?
Back: It reduces parameters and applies the same local feature detector across positions.

Front: CNN foundations and receptive fields: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Confusing channels-first and channels-last layout or shrinking spatial dimensions unexpectedly.

Front: What do recurrent gates control?
Back: How information is retained, updated and exposed in hidden state.

Front: RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs and sequence modeling: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Shuffling tokens within a sequence or treating padding as real observations.

Front: Why divide attention logits by sqrt(d)?
Back: To moderate score magnitude as key dimension grows.

Front: Attention and transformers: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Mask polarity errors and quadratic attention memory for long sequences.

Front: Which architecture is typical for autoregressive chat LLMs?
Back: Decoder-only transformers, though other architectures exist.

Front: Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder architectures: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Assuming every transformer has identical masking or can generate text autoregressively.

Front: What is self-supervised learning?
Back: Learning from supervision constructed from the data itself rather than manual labels.

Front: Transfer learning, embeddings and self-supervised learning: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Training too aggressively can destroy useful pretrained features; domain shift can limit transfer.

Front: What is GAN mode collapse?
Back: The generator produces insufficiently diverse outputs despite plausible individual samples.

Front: Autoencoders, VAEs and GANs: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: A good reconstruction score does not guarantee useful generation; GANs may collapse modes.

Front: What does latent diffusion change?
Back: It performs the diffusion process in a compressed representation rather than directly in pixels.

Front: Diffusion and score-based generative models: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Confusing training noising with inference denoising or assuming fewer steps always preserve quality.

Front: Why is reward design important?
Back: Optimizing a proxy can yield undesirable behavior if it differs from the intended goal.

Front: Reinforcement learning and preference optimization: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Reward hacking, biased preference data and conflating reward with real user value.

Front: What color order does cv2.imread normally use?
Back: BGR for default color images.

Front: Image representation, color spaces and OpenCV: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Displaying BGR as RGB or overflowing uint8 during arithmetic.

Front: What is morphological opening?
Back: Erosion followed by dilation using a structuring element.

Front: Filtering, edges and morphology: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Over-smoothing removes important detail; morphology depends on kernel and polarity.

Front: What does RANSAC do?
Back: Fits a model robustly by testing candidate subsets and selecting strong inlier support.

Front: Geometric transforms, calibration and features: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Homographies fail for many nonplanar scenes; feature matches can contain outliers.

Front: Why split videos by source rather than frames?
Back: Neighboring frames can be near duplicates, inflating validation performance.

Front: Image datasets, augmentation and labeling: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Applying random training augmentations to validation or flipping labels with directional meaning.

Front: What does freezing a backbone do?
Back: Prevents its parameters from updating while the head learns.

Front: Image classification and pretrained CNNs: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Forgetting pretrained input normalization or evaluating only overall accuracy.

Front: What does IoU measure?
Back: Intersection area divided by union area.

Front: Object detection: boxes, IoU, NMS and mAP: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Mixing xyxy and xywh coordinates or comparing mAP computed under different IoU settings.

Front: How does DETR differ from many traditional detectors?
Back: It learns set prediction with matching and commonly avoids conventional NMS.

Front: YOLO, Faster R-CNN, DETR and detection training: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Comparing published speed numbers from different hardware or resolution.

Front: What is the difference between semantic and instance segmentation?
Back: Instance segmentation separates individual objects of the same class.

Front: Semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Including ignored pixels in metrics or using bilinear interpolation for discrete labels.

Front: Why are U-Net skip connections useful?
Back: They recover spatial detail from earlier encoder features.

Front: U-Net, Mask R-CNN, SAM and foundation vision models: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Assuming promptable models are accurate for every domain or using unlicensed imagery.

Front: What is an identity switch?
Back: A tracker assigns a different identity to an object previously tracked under another identity.

Front: Video, optical flow and object tracking: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Ignoring frame-rate variation, occlusion or identity switches.

Front: How does CLIP enable zero-shot classification?
Back: It scores image embeddings against text embeddings for candidate classes.

Front: Vision transformers, CLIP and multimodal vision: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Assuming zero-shot scores are calibrated or ignoring training-data bias.

Front: Why preserve original image coordinates?
Back: Detected regions must map correctly back to the source image.

Front: OCR, document AI, 3D and deployment: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Logging sensitive documents or ignoring coordinate transforms during resizing.

Front: What is a next-token language model trained to predict?
Back: A distribution over the next token given preceding context.

Front: Generative AI landscape and LLM fundamentals: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Equating fluency with factual accuracy or assuming model knowledge is current.

Front: Are tokens equivalent to words?
Back: No; a token may be part of a word, punctuation or another text unit.

Front: Tokens, tokenizers and context windows: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Counting words as tokens or truncating away required evidence and role markers.

Front: What does lower temperature generally do?
Back: Concentrates probability mass on higher-scoring tokens.

Front: Decoding, sampling and inference constraints: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Using low temperature as a correctness guarantee or confusing top-p with top-k.

Front: Why pin a model revision?
Back: To make the artifact and behavior more reproducible.

Front: Hugging Face Hub, Transformers and model selection: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Executing untrusted remote model code or assuming all licenses permit commercial use.

Front: Does one-shot prompting guarantee deterministic output?
Back: No; decoding, infrastructure and model behavior also matter.

Front: Zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Example contamination, order sensitivity and assuming one-shot makes output deterministic.

Front: Why validate even when a provider offers structured output?
Back: Application rules, data provenance and semantic constraints still need checking.

Front: Structured output, few-shot schemas and Pydantic: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Accepting parseable JSON as factual truth or silently coercing invalid values.

Front: Why are generated explanations insufficient as proof?
Back: They can be plausible but inconsistent with the actual facts or computations.

Front: Persona prompting, reasoning prompts and prompt injection: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Trusting a plausible explanation as evidence of correctness or exposing hidden reasoning or secrets.

Front: Are ChatML, Alpaca and INST universal standards?
Back: No; they are model-family conventions with variations.

Front: Prompt serialization: ChatML, Alpaca and INST: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Manually applying the wrong template, duplicating special tokens or concatenating untrusted messages as instructions.

Front: What should a prompt version record include?
Back: Template, model configuration, schema, evaluation dataset and results.

Front: Prompt versioning, testing and context engineering: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Changing model and prompt simultaneously makes attribution difficult.

Front: Is a vector database itself an embedding model?
Back: No; it stores and indexes vectors generated elsewhere.

Front: Embeddings, similarity and vector databases: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Mixing embedding models in one index or missing tenant filters.

Front: Why store source metadata alongside chunks?
Back: To enforce access and provide verifiable citations and lifecycle control.

Front: RAG ingestion, chunking and indexing: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Indexing private content without access metadata or dropping document boundaries.

Front: What is the purpose of a reranker?
Back: Improve relevance ordering among retrieved candidates.

Front: RAG retrieval, reranking and answer grounding: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Using similarity as proof of factual support or citing sources not actually retrieved.

Front: Can an answer be correct but unfaithful?
Back: Yes; it may be correct from prior knowledge without support from retrieved evidence.

Front: RAG evaluation and retrieval diagnostics: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Evaluating only final answer similarity can hide retrieval failure or unsupported claims.

Front: How does original Self-RAG differ from a generic RAG critique loop?
Back: It incorporates learned reflection tokens in the trained model.

Front: Self-reflective RAG and Self-RAG: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Calling any retry loop the original Self-RAG algorithm or trusting a self-grader without validation.

Front: What does CRAG primarily correct?
Back: Poor or uncertain retrieved evidence before generation.

Front: Corrective RAG (CRAG): name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Sending sensitive queries to unapproved search or using corrective results without provenance.

Front: How is answer correction different from retrieval correction?
Back: It targets the generated claims rather than only the retrieved documents.

Front: Self-corrective RAG and iterative verification: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Infinite loops and a judge repeatedly approving its own hallucination.

Front: When is simple RAG preferable?
Back: When one predictable retrieval path handles the task reliably.

Front: Agentic RAG and routing: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Unbounded tool calls, cross-tenant retrieval or unnecessary agency for simple questions.

Front: Who actually executes a tool call?
Back: The application/runtime, after validation and authorization.

Front: Tool calling and tool-use agent pattern: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Executing arbitrary model-generated code or treating tool output as trusted instructions.

Front: What distinguishes ReAct from a fixed chain?
Back: It chooses successive actions based on intermediate observations.

Front: ReAct, planning and action-observation loops: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Infinite repeated actions, stale observations and blindly following tool text.

Front: When should reflection stop?
Back: When acceptance criteria pass, budget expires or escalation is needed.

Front: Reflection and evaluator-optimizer agents: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Self-critique can reinforce errors and add unnecessary cost.

Front: Why not use multiple agents for every task?
Back: They introduce coordination, latency, cost and failure complexity.

Front: Multi-agent systems and orchestration: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Recursive delegation, conflicting writes and sharing unnecessary private context.

Front: What is the benefit of an adapter boundary?
Back: It isolates provider/framework changes from domain logic and tests.

Front: LangChain components and integration boundaries: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Tightly coupling business logic to provider-specific responses or using deprecated examples uncritically.

Front: When is a sequential graph appropriate?
Back: When required stages and their order are known in advance.

Front: LangGraph state, nodes, edges and sequential workflow: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Mutating shared state unexpectedly or placing unrelated data in the graph.

Front: Why are reducers needed for some parallel state fields?
Back: They define how concurrent updates combine rather than overwrite or conflict.

Front: LangGraph conditional and parallel workflows: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Multiple branches updating the same state key without merge semantics.

Front: Why is idempotency important for resumable workflows?
Back: Replayed steps must not repeat harmful external effects.

Front: LangGraph iterative workflows, checkpointing and HITL: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Re-executing a side effect on resume or storing secrets in checkpoint state.

Front: What does MCP standardize?
Back: Interfaces for AI applications to discover and access external capabilities and context.

Front: Model Context Protocol (MCP) fundamentals: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Equating MCP with an agent framework or trusting every discovered capability.

Front: Why prefer typed tool schemas?
Back: They communicate the input contract and enable validation.

Front: FastMCP server and client development: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Exposing filesystem or shell tools without restrictions, or assuming SDK and standalone FastMCP APIs are interchangeable.

Front: Does a tool's advertised description establish trust?
Back: No; server identity, authorization and runtime enforcement establish trust boundaries.

Front: MCP security, remote deployment and interoperability: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Token passthrough without audience validation, prompt injection and SSRF through arbitrary URLs.

Front: How does episodic memory differ from semantic memory?
Back: It represents particular experiences/events rather than general knowledge.

Front: Memory taxonomy: working, factual, episodic and semantic: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Treating every conversation as durable memory or conflating factual and semantic categories as universally disjoint.

Front: Why store timestamps and provenance?
Back: To resolve stale/conflicting facts and support auditing and deletion.

Front: Memory retrieval, summarization and vector storage: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Stale preferences, accidental cross-user retrieval and treating retrieved memory as instructions.

Front: Does a memory library replace an application retention policy?
Back: No; the application must enforce purpose, consent and retention requirements.

Front: Mem0 and persistent agent memory: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Using defaults without understanding external data flow, retaining sensitive data or failing to remove stale memory.

Front: Does async automatically speed up CPU-bound work?
Back: No; it mainly helps overlap waiting for I/O.

Front: FastAPI, Pydantic and async inference APIs: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Blocking an async event loop, returning secrets in exceptions or accepting unbounded requests.

Front: Why include a completion event?
Back: It helps clients distinguish a finished response from an interrupted connection.

Front: Streaming responses: SSE, chunks and cancellation: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Assuming each chunk is valid JSON or leaking unsafe content before moderation completes.

Front: Why use an LLM gateway?
Back: Centralize access, routing, quotas, cost tracking and cross-provider integration.

Front: LiteLLM gateway, routing and fallback: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Retrying non-idempotent side effects or switching models that do not support the required schema.

Front: Why enforce permissions outside the LLM?
Back: The model can be manipulated or mistaken; runtime authorization is authoritative.

Front: Guardrails, prompt injection, privacy and HITL: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Relying solely on an LLM judge or releasing unreviewed streamed content.

Front: Why randomize answer order in pairwise judging?
Back: To detect or reduce position bias.

Front: Agent evaluation, datasets and LLM-as-judge: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Using the same model as generator and uncalibrated sole evaluator or exposing private traces to judges.

Front: Why separate offline and judge-backed tests?
Back: Offline tests are stable and inexpensive; semantic judging is variable and may cost money.

Front: DeepEval for LLM and agent regression tests: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Confusing metric thresholds with universal quality standards or depending on live models for all unit tests.

Front: What does faithfulness aim to measure?
Back: Whether answer claims are supported by supplied context.

Front: Ragas for RAG evaluation: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Using an unavailable reference field or comparing metrics across changed evaluator configurations.

Front: Why test prompts against a fixed fixture set?
Back: To detect regressions when templates or providers change.

Front: Promptfoo for prompt/model evaluation and red teaming: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Storing API keys in YAML or attacking systems without authorization.

Front: What does p95 latency mean?
Back: 95% of measured requests complete at or below that duration.

Front: Observability, traces, evaluation gates and cost: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Logging secrets or using aggregate metrics that hide high-risk failures.

Front: What is LoRA's central idea?
Back: Learn a low-rank weight update while keeping the base weights frozen.

Front: Fine-tuning datasets, SFT and PEFT/LoRA: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Training on benchmark answers, poor data formatting or assuming fine-tuning adds reliable current facts.

Front: What does the KV cache store?
Back: Attention key/value states for previously processed tokens to avoid recomputation.

Front: QLoRA, quantization, serving and model optimization: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Assuming four-bit storage equals complete runtime memory or every GPU supports every kernel.

Front: When is RAG preferable to fine-tuning for changing facts?
Back: When facts must be retrieved and updated independently with traceable evidence.

Front: Multimodal LLMs, diffusion apps and fine-tuning decisions: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Treating fine-tuning as a replacement for retrieval or submitting private images to unapproved providers.

Front: Why package preprocessing with a model?
Back: To avoid train-serving skew.

Front: Model packaging, APIs and Docker: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Loading untrusted pickle/joblib artifacts or training on service startup.

Front: What is the difference between a run and a model version?
Back: A run records an experiment; a version identifies a registered model artifact.

Front: MLflow, data versioning and experiment tracking: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Storing sensitive data in experiment metadata or promoting based on training score.

Front: Why gate deployment on model quality as well as code tests?
Back: Correct software can still serve a degraded or unsafe model.

Front: CI/CD, continuous training and DevSecOps: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Automatically promoting a retrained model without comparing it to a baseline.

Front: Can data drift occur without concept drift?
Back: Yes; input distribution can change while the target relationship stays stable.

Front: Monitoring, drift, reliability and retraining: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Treating every detected shift as concept drift or retraining automatically without verification.

Front: What should a model card communicate?
Back: Intended use, evaluation, limitations, data considerations and known risks.

Front: Responsible AI, governance and security: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Assuming public data is always licensed for training or logging full user conversations.

Front: Why separate ingestion and online inference?
Back: They have different resource, latency and scaling characteristics.

Front: Cloud architecture, scaling and deployment trade-offs: name a common failure to avoid.
Back: Overprovisioning GPUs, exposing indexes publicly or scaling without measurement.
